correctness.rationale: For two distinct positive queries, disjoint edges have at most one common center (two bridges force a triangle or square); incident edges leave only their common star, in which a new query isolates or co-isolates at most one center. This precludes online depth four. After a positive root uv, queries outside both endpoints hit at most one candidate and queries through u other than uv hit just the other u-edges, excluding themselves. A depth-two split of this positive space therefore requires degree at least four at one endpoint and at least two at the other. That proves the subcubic cap and supplies a fixed shattered pair: two edges a,b at the high-degree endpoint have traces 01,10,11,00 from a,b,uv and an extension at the opposite endpoint. The general lower bound VC <= Ldim and the depth-one case cover the remaining dimensions, including the empty-class convention. The exact nine-vertex depth-three certificate checks out; depth three requires eight distinct edge functions, excluding all smaller trees.
residual_risks: Finite replay establishes the two witnesses, not the all-graph bounds; the latter follow from the incidence proof. No claim for graphs with triangles or squares.

value.rationale: These are sharp structural thresholds for adaptive edge identification: maximum degree alone excludes depth three below four, and girth forces the adaptive advantage over fixed queries to at most one. The P5 and minimum-order nine-vertex tree show that the advantage is genuine even among trees and certify where the higher online rank starts; the result is not a computation of two arbitrary trees.
residual_risks: No exact rank classification of individual girth-five graphs or broader line graph families is claimed.
